pages.hook: Kansas City is famous for barbecue: meat cooked slowly, with a sweet, thick sauce. In a barbecue place, friends often share one big plate and eat with their hands.
pages.polite: Ask **What’s good here?** and say **We’ll share this one.** Say **Dig in!** when the food comes.

mythfact.s: Kansas City is well known for barbecue.
mythfact.why: Ribs, brisket and “burnt ends” are local favorites.

mythfact.s: Barbecue in the USA is only chicken.
mythfact.why: Pork, beef and chicken are all common, and each region has its own style.

mythfact.s: It is normal to eat ribs with your hands.
mythfact.why: Most people eat ribs by hand and use napkins.

mythfact.s: Restaurants never give you “sides”.
mythfact.why: Sides like corn, beans and coleslaw are very common with barbecue.

mythfact.s: Barbecue sauce is often sweet and a little smoky.
mythfact.why: Kansas City sauce is known for being thick and sweet.

decode.q: How much are a rack of ribs and two sides?

lines: Wash your hands before you eat

compare.br: In Brazil, a churrasco is a social meal with many cuts of meat, often shared at home or at a churrascaria.
compare.us: In the USA, a barbecue place serves big plates to share, with sides and sauce; it is casual and messy.
compare.tip: Say “Can we share?” and “Extra napkins, please!”
compare.ask: Do you share food with friends? What do you share? Say it in English.

pages.title: Cultural spotlight · Quiz
Reading quest — Ribs in Kansas City · part 1
text: My friend Carl and I went to a barbecue restaurant in **Kansas City**. It smelled so good! A man called Aaron said, “**Welcome! Do you want to share?**” “Yes,” we said. “**What’s good here?**”
“**The ribs are great**,” said Aaron. We ordered one rack of ribs. Then he asked, “**Do you want sides?**” “Corn and beans, please,” I said. “**Anything to drink?**” “Two waters, please.”

The food came on one big plate. There was no knife and no fork, only napkins! Carl said, “**Dig in!**” We ate the ribs with our hands. The sauce was sweet and a little smoky. It was “**finger-lickin’ good**”, and we laughed.

pages.title: Reading quest — Ribs in Kansas City · part 2
text: I remembered a nursery rhyme from England, “Little Jack Horner”. It is from about the 1700s. A boy sits in a corner and eats a Christmas pie. He pulls out a plum and says, “What a good boy am I!” We sat at a corner table too, and I felt like Jack Horner.
At the end, Carl said, “**I’m stuffed!**” I said, “**Save room** for dessert.” We shared a small piece of pie. It was a perfect lunch, and we will come back soon.
